transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess I came in because I just can’t seem to stop worrying. It’s like everything is stacked up in my head at the same time—my marriage, work, bills, stuff around the house I keep starting and not finishing.

I work with computers, so I’m used to juggling a lot of things, but this feels different. Like I’ll be thinking about one work issue, and then suddenly I’m thinking, “Am I messing up at work? Am I letting everyone down?” And then it jumps to whether I’m being a bad husband or father, and then the bills, and then some project in the garage I haven’t touched in weeks. I know that probably sounds all over the place—sorry. That’s kind of the problem. I feel like I’m failing at everything at once.
Do you find that these worries come up even when there’s no immediate problem to solve, or do they usually happen in response to specific situations?

It comes up even when there isn’t really anything happening right that second. Like, I’ll just be sitting there and suddenly my brain is running through everything—my marriage, whether I’m slipping at work, bills, stuff around the house I’ve started and then dropped. 

And then I start thinking I’m basically failing as a husband and a father, and it all piles on at once. It’s not like one clear problem I can just solve and be done with. It’s more like my mind keeps opening new tabs, if that makes sense… and then I can’t close any of them.
Do you notice any physical feelings when these worries come up, like restlessness, muscle tension, or trouble relaxing?

Yeah… definitely. I feel kind of wound tight almost all day, like my shoulders are locked up or I’m bracing for something even when nothing’s happening.

I notice it at work a lot—between meetings I’ll get up and pace around, and I’ll tell myself I’m just “thinking,” but really sitting still feels almost impossible. Even at chess club, which is supposed to be relaxing, I catch myself tapping pieces or fidgeting with them instead of just… playing normally. It’s like my body is waiting for something bad to drop.
Have you noticed feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, like hobbies or time with family?

Um… I don’t know. I mean, I still do things, I think. Like I still go through the motions with family stuff and hobbies and all that, but it’s hard to tell what’s “not interested” versus just being distracted, you know?

Like I’ll sit down with something I normally enjoy and then my mind wanders off to some random thing I forgot to do, or something at work, and then I realize I haven’t really been paying attention. But I wouldn’t say I feel… hopeless exactly. Down? Maybe sometimes, but I don’t know if that’s the main thing. It’s more like I can’t get settled enough to enjoy anything the way I used to.

Sorry, I’m not sure if that answers it.
Have you been feeling more tired than usual or noticed a drop in your energy levels, even when you haven’t been doing anything particularly demanding?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I do feel worn out sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s “more tired than usual” or just… normal adult life, you know? I sit at a computer most of the day, and somehow that can make you feel drained even though you haven’t physically done anything.

Like yesterday I got home and just kind of stood in the kitchen looking at the mail, and then I started thinking about how we need a better system for sorting it because there are always piles, and then that reminded me of this drawer in the hallway that’s basically just batteries and old receipts—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

Energy-wise… I don’t know. I haven’t noticed a clear drop, I guess. It’s hard for me to separate being tired from just being mentally busy.
Do you feel like you’re able to control these worries, or do they seem to take over even when you try to focus on something else?

Yeah, it… it takes over. I try to tell myself, like, “Just focus on the code in front of you,” and for maybe thirty seconds I can, but then one concern grabs onto another one.

Like if I think, “What if this project isn’t good enough,” then suddenly I’m imagining a bad review, and then that turns into losing my job, and then I’m thinking about how my family would be worse off because of me. And I know that’s a lot of steps, and I can kind of see that it’s spiraling, but stopping it is a different thing.

Even when I’m trying to work out and just breathe or count reps or whatever, my brain keeps pulling me back into it. It’s like I can redirect it, but I can’t really keep it redirected.
Have you noticed yourself getting more irritable or easily annoyed lately, even over small things?

I’m… not sure, honestly. I mean, I get annoyed, but I don’t know if it’s more than usual or just because little things pile up.

Like if something small happens—someone leaving a dish out or an email coming in with no clear subject line—I can feel myself tense up for a second, but then I also start thinking, well, maybe that’s just normal, because who doesn’t get irritated by that? And then I’ll remember I still need to clean out the fridge, which is unrelated, sorry.

So… I don’t know that I’ve noticed a clear change. Maybe a little, but I can’t really say for sure.
Have you felt like things are hopeless or that you're not able to see a way forward, even in areas of your life that used to feel manageable?

I don’t… I don’t think I’d say hopeless, exactly. I mean, sometimes things feel really tangled, like I can’t see the next step clearly, but that’s not the same as thinking there’s no way forward, right?

Like with work stuff, I’ll get stuck thinking through every possible outcome, and then I’ll end up reorganizing my notes or opening ten tabs about some completely unrelated tool—actually yesterday I spent way too long looking at keyboard trays, which has nothing to do with anything.

But hopeless… no, I’m not sure that’s the word I’d use. More like overwhelmed, maybe. I can usually still imagine that things could get sorted out, even if in the moment it feels messy.
Have you felt like nothing really brings you joy anymore, even things you used to enjoy?

I don’t know if I’d say nothing brings me joy anymore. That feels… too absolute, maybe.

I mean, I still like things sometimes. Like if I’m messing around with a side project or watching something funny, I can enjoy it for a bit. But then I start thinking about whether I’m wasting time, or if I should be doing laundry, or if the thing I’m watching is actually even good—sorry, that’s not really the point.

So… no, I haven’t noticed that everything feels joyless. It’s more that I have trouble staying with it, I guess. But I wouldn’t say nothing brings me joy.
Have you noticed that activities you used to enjoy don’t feel as rewarding or pleasurable as they used to, even when you’re not worrying about other things?

I’m not totally sure. I don’t think I’ve noticed it in that specific way.

Like, if I’m doing something I usually like, I can still get something out of it, but then I start kind of analyzing whether I’m enjoying it enough, which probably defeats the purpose. And then I’ll drift into thinking about something else entirely—like whether I replied to a message or why my desk drawer keeps sticking, which is not really relevant.

But if you mean, when I’m actually not caught up in other thoughts, does it still feel less pleasurable… I don’t know. I haven’t really been able to separate it that cleanly. I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed that, no.
Have you noticed that even when you’re not worrying, things don’t feel as enjoyable or satisfying as they used to?

I’m not sure I can tell, honestly. Like, the “even when I’m not worrying” part is hard for me to separate out, because I’ll be doing something and then suddenly I’m thinking about whether I’m doing it the right way or whether I should be doing something else.

But when I’m actually just… in it, I don’t know that I’ve noticed things feeling flat or unsatisfying in that way. Like, I can still enjoy a good meal or a funny video or messing with some little tech thing—actually I spent an embarrassing amount of time comparing monitor arms the other day, which is not really a hobby but kind of became one.

So, I guess no, I haven’t clearly noticed that things don’t feel enjoyable anymore. It’s more that I get pulled out of them.
Have you had trouble falling asleep or staying asleep, even when you’re physically tired?

Yeah. That’s actually been… pretty bad.

Most nights I’ll be physically exhausted, like I can barely keep my eyes open on the couch, and then the second I’m in bed my brain just turns on. I start running through work stuff—risks, things I might’ve missed, some email I should’ve worded differently. And then it jumps to money, or something I said to my wife that maybe came out wrong.

And even when I do fall asleep, I’ll wake up around 3 or 4, and it’s like I’m immediately back in problem-solving mode. I’ll already be rehearsing tomorrow, what could go wrong, what I need to do first… and then I can’t get back down. It’s frustrating, because I am tired. I’m just not… off.
Would you say that you worry excessively or feel anxious about a range of things most days, and has this been going on for at least several months?

Yeah… I mean, that’s basically why I came in. It feels like I can’t stop worrying about everything at once.

It’s my marriage, and then whether I’m slipping at work, and bills, and the house stuff I keep starting and then dropping halfway through—like there’s this cabinet thing that’s been sitting there for weeks, which sounds stupid, but every time I see it I’m like, “Great, another thing I’m failing at.”

And then it all sort of turns into this bigger thing of, am I just not doing well enough as a husband, as a father… as an adult, I guess. So yes, most days it’s there. It’s not just one topic. It kind of jumps around and piles up.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's reason for seeking psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with excessive anxiety and worry about multiple domains occurring more days than not for at least several months, accompanied by associated symptoms including restlessness, difficulty concentrating, and sleep disturbance. These symptoms are not better explained by an adjustment disorder, as the anxiety is more persistent and not limited to a reaction to a specific stressor.
